title: Reliable Trade Order Processing
summary: Accept buy and sell orders quickly with a stable order ID.
Persist order state before any asynchronous execution begins.
Make retries safe while scaling to 5,000 requests per second.

sections.title: Understanding
points: The API accepts buy or sell orders and returns quickly with an order ID.
Every accepted order must be durable and observable through a status endpoint.
The system must prevent duplicate execution at 5,000 requests per second despite provider failures.
speakingNotes: I would clarify that quick API response means acknowledgement, not synchronous execution.
The order ID and status contract let users follow progress after the request returns.
The hardest requirement is safe recovery when an external provider may have accepted an order before timing out.

sections.title: Approach
points: Use a stateless API to validate, authenticate, and durably accept each order.
Separate order acceptance from execution with a transactional outbox and durable queue.
Treat execution as an idempotent state machine with explicit recovery for ambiguous outcomes.
speakingNotes: The API path should do only validation and the minimum durable write needed to accept the order.
The outbox prevents a committed order from being lost if the service crashes before publishing work.
Workers can retry, but they must reconcile an uncertain provider result before sending again.

sections.title: Core Solution
points: Store orders with a unique client idempotency key and an explicit state machine in PostgreSQL.
Commit the order and an outbox event in one transaction, then publish the event to a durable queue.
Workers claim orders with leases and send the provider the same idempotency key on every retry.
On a timeout, reconcile with the provider before retrying; record execution and status transitions durably.
speakingNotes: A unique constraint makes concurrent duplicate submissions return the original order rather than create another one.
At-least-once delivery is acceptable when both the worker and the provider call are idempotent.
The ambiguous timeout state is important: blindly retrying could execute a trade twice.
sections.visual:
flowchart LR
  Client --> API
  API --> Orders[(PostgreSQL)]
  API --> Outbox[(Outbox)]
  Outbox --> Queue[(Durable Queue)]
  Queue --> Worker
  Worker --> Provider[Execution Provider]
  Worker --> Reconcile[Reconcile]
  Reconcile --> Provider
  Worker --> Orders

sections.title: Verification
points: Test concurrent duplicate requests, duplicate queue messages, worker crashes, and lease expiry.
Test provider success, rejection, timeout after acceptance, and repeated reconciliation.
Load test 5,000 requests per second and monitor API latency, queue lag, database saturation, and stuck orders.
speakingNotes: I would test the crash windows around the database commit, queue publish, and provider response.
The most important assertion is one business execution, even when the same message is delivered repeatedly.
Capacity testing must include the database and provider limits, not only the API tier.

sections.title: Wrap-up
points: Return quickly from a durable acceptance path, then process execution asynchronously.
Use idempotency, reconciliation, and explicit unknown states to make partial failures safe.
Scale stateless APIs and workers independently, while keeping PostgreSQL the order-state source of truth.
speakingNotes: The design prioritises durable acceptance and safe recovery over pretending every network call is exactly once.
True no-duplicate execution requires the provider to support idempotency or a reliable reconciliation API.
I would start with this flow, measure queue and provider bottlenecks, and scale the independent tiers as needed.
